title: “Disrespectful for Voters”: The Dakotas Weigh Raising the Bar for Direct Democracy
author: Pascal Sabino
content:
Over 50,000 South Dakotans became eligible for Medicaid [three years
ago](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/press-releases/south-dakota-expands-
medicaid-bringing-health-coverage-more-52000-state-residents) thanks to a
constitutional amendment to vastly expand health care coverage that voters
approved in 2022. Despite opposition from the Republicans who control South
Dakota’s government, supporters brought the Medicaid initiative to the ballot
and passed it with over 56 percent of the vote.

But in future cycles, initiatives that win that same level of support could
fail to be enacted. Republican lawmakers placed a measure on the ballot this
fall that would raise the bar for amending the state constitution from 50 to
60 percent. All four amendments approved by voters since 2020, including the
Medicaid expansion, have fallen short of that threshold.

Advocates who have worked on prior initiatives warn that the proposal, which
will appear on the ballot as [Amendment
L](https://ballotpedia.org/South_Dakota_Constitutional_Amendment_L,_60%25_Vote_Requirement_for_Constitutional_Amendments_Measure_\(2026\)),
would undermine the power of voters to enact reforms when legislators refuse
to do so. Rick Weiland, co-chair of Dakotans for Health, a grassroots network
that campaigned for the 2022 Medicaid expansion, says that Republicans, who
currently hold 97 out of the 105 seats in South Dakota’s legislature, are
pushing to change the rules because they resent that their control can still
be “circumvented by the initiative process.”

“Voters in South Dakota enjoy the fact that if we don’t like what is going on
in the capital, we can do something about it. But there are efforts every
session to try to completely neuter the process,” Weiland told _Bolts_. “It’s
a death by a thousand cuts.”

This November, South Dakota is one of the two states that will be voting on
near-identical measures to raise the threshold for approving any
constitutional amendment to 60 percent. Republicans are championing the same
change in neighboring North Dakota.

North Dakota’s leaders have also grown frustrated at recent popular
initiatives that have managed to bypass the legislature. Voters in 2018
created an [ethics commission](https://www.propublica.org/article/north-
dakota-ethics-commission-enforcement-authority) to investigate corruption by
public officials, and in 2022 they set term limits for the governor and
legislators. “You aren’t going to have politicians lead the charge on term
limits themselves,” said state Representative Jared Hendrix, a Republican [who
spearheaded](https://www.inforum.com/news/north-dakota/north-dakota-term-
limits-group-sues-jaeger-over-rejected-signatures) the 2022 initiative on term
limits before he was elected to the legislature. He now opposes the upcoming
[referendum](https://ballotpedia.org/North_Dakota_Constitutional_Measure_1,_60%25_Vote_Requirement_for_Constitutional_Amendments_Measure_\(2026\)).

These proposals add to a [broad national push](https://boltsmag.org/direct-
democracy-roundtable-ohio-arkansas-idaho/) by Republican officials
[in](https://boltsmag.org/oklahoma-restricts-ballot-initiative-process/)
[red](https://boltsmag.org/new-rules-from-gop-legislature-target-arkansas-
ballot-initiatives/) [states](https://boltsmag.org/florida-new-restrictions-
on-ballot-initiative-process/) to restrict direct democracy, which remains a
rare path forward for popular reforms the GOP opposes. They’ve passed laws
that make it more difficult to qualify measures for the ballot, including by
[criminalizing](https://boltsmag.org/florida-new-restrictions-on-ballot-
initiative-process/) routine signature gathering methods with harsh
punishments for missed deadlines and clerical errors.

Still, when voters have weighed in on new restrictions, they have
[typically](https://boltsmag.org/arizona-results-of-democracy-measures-
prop-134-136-and-137/) [rejected](https://boltsmag.org/ohio-ballot-
issue-1-abortion-direct-democracy-ballot-initiative/) them. Just this month,
Missourians overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have [forced
initiatives to](https://boltsmag.org/missouri-amendment-on-ballot-
initiatives/) pass in every congressional district—a geographic supermajority
of sorts.

In the Dakotas, too, voters have kept killing past proposals meant to weaken
direct democracy.

In 2014, North Dakotans shut down attempts to ban popular initiatives that
require spending public funds. In 2020, they blocked a proposal that would
have required that initiatives first be submitted to lawmakers for approval.
And in 2024, they rejected a measure that would have raised the number of
signatures a petition must collect to qualify for the ballot.

And South Dakotans have twice refused to impose a supermajority on ballot
measures, in
[2018](https://ballotpedia.org/South_Dakota_Constitutional_Amendment_X,_55%25_Vote_Requirement_to_Approve_Constitutional_Amendments_Measure_\(2018\))
and then again [in 2022](https://boltsmag.org/south-dakota-amendment-c-result-
medicaid/). Republicans rushed that second measure in the summer of 2022 in
hopes of [blocking the Medicaid amendment](https://boltsmag.org/amendment-c-
south-dakota-medicaid/), which was ultimately approved later that year.

“This is the third time in about eight years that our legislature has
attempted to make it more difficult for citizens to use direct democracy
methods,” says Chase Jensen, the organizing director of Dakota Rural Action, a
South Dakota-based organization that supported the popular initiative to
expand Medicaid.

“The last two attempts both failed by wide margins, and so having a third
attempt here is more than just annoying,” he added. “It feels disrespectful
for the voters of South Dakota, who have already spoken very clearly.”

In addition to the Dakotas, two states will vote on measures this fall that
would impose supermajorities specifically on citizen-led ballot measures that
create new taxes. Republican legislators are [proposing the change in
Utah](https://www.multistate.us/elections/ballot-measure?id=245). In
California, the November measure was advanced by the Democratic-run
legislature as a [compromise](https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-
government/capitol-alert/article316274423.html) with a conservative advocacy
group that was planning a proposal that cracked down even further on tax
initiatives; the Democrat who sponsored the measure in the legislature [is now
urging voters to reject
it](https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/ballot-measure-
constitutional-amendment-wicks-22330312.php).

This year’s measures in the Dakotas would change rules for any and all
constitutional amendments, whether an amendment is initiated directly by the
people or placed on the ballot by legislators.

South Dakota Representative John Hughes, a Republican who is leading the push
for new rules in that state, argues that the bar for constitutional amendments
should be much higher than for passing ordinary laws. The state’s constitution
is meant to be a framework for “the rights, duties and values that we hold
to,” he said at a House committee meeting last year.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/471192472_1008530447968950_8549873797342003467_n-e1784131141481.jpg)An
organizer in South Dakota assists with efforts to collect citizen petitions
(photo via Dakotans for Health/Facebook).

Hughes also said the simple majority currently needed to approve amendments
has made the state a magnet for out-of-state interest groups seeking to sway
voters. He complains that a large share of the funds behind a 2024 [abortion
access
initiative](https://ballotpedia.org/South_Dakota_Constitutional_Amendment_G,_Right_to_Abortion_Initiative_\(2024\)),
which did not pass, came from donors outside of South Dakota.

“There is a weariness and a fatigue over deceptive ads paid for by millions of
out-of-state dollars to reshape and remold our constitution,” Hughes said at
the hearing. “It is only because we have the 50 percent plus one majority that
we are a target for being used as a laboratory for the emergence of new values
and new ideas that many, many, many South Dakotans do not share.”

But South Dakota advocates who oppose Amendment L say it is already difficult
to amend the state constitution.

In order to qualify a constitutional amendment on the ballot, organizers must
collect twice as many signatures as they would for a regular popular
initiative: 10 percent of the number of votes cast in the latest gubernatorial
race, which is over 35,000 signatures this year. Plus, Jensen said, most
people default to voting against an initiative unless they understand the
issue and it resonates with them, which makes any campaign an expensive and
uphill battle.

“It would definitely create a rule of the minority situation where it would be
nearly impossible, or it would become _so_ expensive to make anything happen,”
he said.

Hendrix, the North Dakota lawmaker who led the 2022 campaign for term limits,
also rejects the claim that the bar to amending his state’s constitution is
too low. To make it on the ballot, his campaign [had to sue state
officials](https://www.inforum.com/news/north-dakota/term-limits-initiative-
will-appear-on-north-dakota-ballot-supreme-court-rules) after they rejected
the signatures for the term limits initiative.

“I agree that it should not be easy to change our constitution, but I would
say that it's generally not easy,” he told _Bolts_. “It should still be an
avenue that we can use with reasonable guardrails.”

Critics of the proposed supermajorities also say amending a state constitution
can be essential to prevent state lawmakers from rolling back a popular
initiative they don’t like.

Utah’s supreme court in 2024 [restricted](https://boltsmag.org/utah-supreme-
court-direct-democracy/) lawmakers’ ability to just ignore the results of a
popular initiative, but many states lack such protections. In South Dakota,
voters in 2016 enacted an anti-corruption reform to create an independent
ethics commission to oversee compliance with campaign finance and lobbying
rules. But that initiative only changed ordinary statutes rather than amend
the constitution, and legislators repealed it three months later.

They “couldn’t keep their hands off of it,” Weiland told _Bolts._

South Dakota’s Republican officials have so far been unable to cancel the 2022
measure that expanded Medicaid since that initiative amended the state
constitution.  

This year, they’ve advanced a constitutional amendment to weaken the Medicaid
expansion, but they need voters to sign off on the change. That item, which
will also appear on the ballot in November as [Amendment
I](https://ballotpedia.org/South_Dakota_Constitutional_Amendment_I,_Medicaid_Expansion_Conditioned_on_90%25_Federal_Funding_Amendment_\(2026\)),
would repeal the 2022 expansion if the federal government ever reimburses less
than 90 percent of Medicaid costs. Currently, South Dakota adults who earn up
to 138 percent of the federal poverty line are eligible for Medicaid, which is
$45,540 for a family of four. The repeal would make non-disabled individuals
ineligible and it would include only people with children that earn below 46
percent of the poverty line, or $15,180 for a family of four.

“They have been looking at different ways of trying to get rid of Medicaid
expansion in the state since it was passed popularly by the voters,” said
Jensen, of Dakota Rural Action.

South Dakota was the first state in the nation to create a system of direct
democracy when it established an initiative process [in
1898](https://aberdeenmag.com/2019/01/father-haire/). Proponents saw it as a
way to balance against the corporate interests that had come to dominate the
legislature as new railroad development brought industry to the region.

Since then, that pathway for civic groups to be directly involved in lawmaking
has remained an essential part of South Dakota’s political identity,
“especially since we have a single party rule for a very long time,” said
Jensen. He hopes that this means voters will reject the latest effort to
restrict this pathway.

“A lot of people were upset about the way that our decision makers were not
representing the will of the people, and there's a lot of that same sentiment
around today,” he said. “So I don't anticipate anybody is excited to give up
one of their rights in our state.”
